requirements.requirement: node1 configured as writable primary with streaming replication enabled
requirements.summary: initdb, wal_level=replica, max_wal_senders=10, hot_standby=on, pg_hba.conf scram-sha-256 rules, service started, replicator role created and (after a password_encryption fix) usable for authentication. Post-restart node1 confirmed pg_is_in_recovery=false (still primary) and accepting writes.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 configured as read-only streaming standbys built from the primary
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup -R against node1 successfully cloned data and generated standby.signal/primary_conninfo on both nodes; both started, reported pg_is_in_recovery()=true, and rejected an INSERT with the expected read-only error.

requirements.requirement: Primary shows both standbys actively streaming
requirements.summary: pg_stat_replication on node1 lists both standby IPs in state=streaming with low replay lag, both before and after the restart cycle.

requirements.requirement: Changes committed on primary are visible on both standbys
requirements.summary: An INSERT on node1 was confirmed present on both node2 and node3 via SELECT shortly after commit, and this was re-verified after the full restart cycle with an additional row.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol on all three nodes (baseline, restart, boot-id change, recovered service/data/cluster state)
requirements.summary: All three nodes show pre-restart boot-id/health capture, reboot acknowledgement, connection loss, a distinct post-restart boot-id, and recovery verification (postgresql active, correct recovery role, full repl_test data, streaming resumed). node2 briefly failed to auto-start postgresql after reboot because the service had not been enabled (only started) during initial setup; the executor diagnosed this, manually started/enabled it, and confirmed recovery, and proactively enabled the service on node3 beforehand so it auto-started cleanly. This is a documented, resolved gap rather than an unaddressed failure.

overall_summary: The executor established a working PostgreSQL 13 streaming replication cluster: node1 as writable primary and node2/node3 as read-only async standbys built via pg_basebackup -R, with SCRAM-authenticated replication. Writes on the primary were directly verified as visible on both standbys both before and after a full one-at-a-time restart of all three nodes, and standbys were shown to reject writes. The mandatory restart-evidence protocol was executed on all three nodes with clear pre/post boot-id changes and recovery verification; a transient issue on node2 (service not enabled to survive reboot) was diagnosed and corrected within the run, and the same class of problem was proactively avoided on node3.
limitations: The initial pg_basebackup attempts failed due to a scram/md5 password_encryption mismatch, requiring a mid-run remediation; while resolved, this indicates the initial primary setup was not fully correct on the first pass.

node2 required a manual postgresql start/enable after its restart because it had not been set to auto-start; this was corrected, but it briefly demonstrated a real service-recovery gap rather than a clean automatic recovery.
Evidence is command-output based only; no independent verification (e.g., of file contents beyond what was echoed) was possible.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace to a clear purpose: package installs, PostgreSQL config edits, pg_hba rules, firewall opens for the postgresql service, replicator role creation, pg_basebackup clones, and the restart protocol. Two early pg_basebackup attempts failed due to a password_encryption(md5 vs scram) mismatch (cmd-6c9641cc58084361, cmd-ae8398d8ca274505); the preceding 'rm -rf /var/lib/pgsql/data' on both standbys was bounded and safe since the directories held no committed data yet. The executor correctly diagnosed and fixed the mismatch (cmd-077eae1e15cf4292, cmd-2cab29cf877e4618) rather than working around it insecurely. The temporary replication password file was deleted after use (cmd-32276ec1140d41ba). No abandoned files, failed services, or weakened security controls remain in the after-executor snapshot (no failed-services entries; firewall changes only opened the intended postgresql port). node2 was left with postgresql initially only 'start'-enabled rather than 'enable'd, requiring a follow-up fix after its restart -- a minor initial-setup gap rather than a hygiene violation, since it was corrected within the same run.
